title: Loop Safety: budgets, timeouts & stopping
summary: An autonomous agent decides its own next step, so without guardrails it can loop forever, burn a fortune in tokens, or hang on a slow call. Loop safety is the set of controls that bound every run: a max-step cap, token/time budgets, no-progress detection, an explicit done signal, and a hard cost cap. Every production agent loop needs all of them — they are the difference between a controllable system and a runaway one.

subtopics.title: Cap the number of steps
subtopics.explanation: The simplest and most important guardrail is a hard maximum on loop iterations, so even a confused agent that never emits 'done' stops after a bounded number of turns. You loop over range(MAX_STEPS) rather than while True, and treat hitting the cap as a real, handled outcome. A step cap alone turns 'might run forever' into 'runs at most N times', which is the floor of loop safety.

subtopics.title: Bound tokens and wall-clock time
subtopics.explanation: Steps aren't the only thing that grows: each turn adds tokens and seconds, so you also track a running token budget and a deadline and stop when either is exceeded. A few steps with huge context can cost more than many small ones, and a single slow tool can blow the latency budget. Token and time budgets bound the two resources a step count can't see on its own.

subtopics.title: Detect when the agent stops making progress
subtopics.explanation: An agent can stay under every budget yet spin uselessly — repeating the same action or oscillating between two with no new information. No-progress detection tracks recent actions or state and halts when nothing is changing, catching loops far earlier than the raw step cap. Stopping a stuck run early saves the tokens and time it would otherwise waste circling.

subtopics.title: Require an explicit done signal
subtopics.explanation: Stopping should be a deliberate act, not an accident of running out of budget: give the model a clear way to declare completion — a finish/submit tool or a final_answer field — and treat only that as a clean success. Everything else (cap, budget, no-progress) is a fallback stop that the caller handles differently. An explicit done signal separates 'the agent finished the task' from 'we forcibly cut it off'.

subtopics.title: Put a hard cap on cost
subtopics.explanation: Because tokens map to money, a runaway or adversarial run can rack up real spend, so a cost cap — derived from the token budget or tracked per run and per user — is the last line of defense. You estimate spend as you go and abort when it crosses a ceiling, ideally with alerts before the hard limit. A cost cap is what keeps a single bad run, or a prompt-injection loop, from producing a shocking bill.

foundations.overview: An agent loop is unusual software: it decides its own control flow, so nothing outside the loop guarantees it ever stops. Loop safety is the layered set of guardrails that bound every run. The floor is a max-step cap — looping over a fixed range instead of while True so a confused agent halts after N turns. On top of that sit token and time budgets, because steps hide two growing resources: context tokens (which cost money) and wall-clock latency (which a slow tool can blow). No-progress detection catches the subtler failure where the agent stays within budget but spins — repeating or oscillating actions with no new information — and halts it early. An explicit done signal (a finish tool or final_answer field) makes stopping intentional, cleanly separating 'the task is complete' from 'we forcibly cut it off'. Finally a hard cost cap, derived from tokens, is the last line of defense against a runaway or prompt-injection loop producing a shocking bill. Every forced stop is a handled outcome the caller can route — to a human, a fallback, or a safe default — never an unhandled crash or an infinite loop. Together these controls turn an autonomous system from a runaway risk into something bounded and operable.
foundations.formalDefinition: Loop safety is the collection of termination and resource guardrails on an autonomous agent loop: a maximum step count, token and wall-clock budgets, no-progress (repetition/oscillation) detection, an explicit completion signal distinguishing clean success from forced stops, and a cost ceiling — each of which, when exceeded, halts the loop with a handled, routable outcome.
foundations.whyItMatters: Because the agent chooses its own next action, an ungoverned loop can run forever, exhaust context, hang on a dependency, or burn unbounded money — and a single prompt injection or model mistake can trigger any of these unattended. Loop safety is what makes an autonomous agent affordable, predictable, and safe to run in production rather than a liability.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of sending a contractor to fix your house with an open-ended brief. You still set a deadline (time budget), a spending limit (cost cap), a cap on the number of trips they make (max steps), and you ask them to tell you explicitly when the job is done (done signal) — and if you notice them redoing the same wall over and over (no progress), you call it off. The guardrails aren't distrust of the contractor; they're how you keep any open-ended job bounded.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding agents capped at N tool calls and a token budget per task, research agents with a wall-clock deadline and cost ceiling per query, support agents that must emit an explicit resolve/escalate action to finish, and any hosted agent platform enforcing per-run and per-user spend limits with alerting.
commonUseCases: Capping steps so a non-terminating agent still halts
Detecting and breaking no-progress repetition loops
Per-run and per-user cost caps with alerts

commonMisconceptions.myth: A step cap is enough loop safety on its own.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A step cap bounds iterations but not tokens, time, or money — a few huge-context steps can be slow and expensive. You need budgets and a cost cap alongside it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Hitting a limit is an error to throw.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A forced stop is an expected outcome to handle and route (to a human, fallback, or default), not an unhandled exception. Clean success comes only from an explicit done signal.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If it's under budget, the agent is fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: An agent can stay within every budget while spinning uselessly on repeated actions. No-progress detection is what catches that waste before the budget does.

interactiveExamples.explanation: One loop enforces three guardrails at once: a max-step cap, a running cost cap, and a clean stop only on an explicit finish action. A fake model finishes on step 3, well inside the limits, and the result reports exactly why it stopped.

interactiveExamples.title: No-progress detection stops a spinning agent early
interactiveExamples.explanation: This agent stays far under the step cap and any budget but repeats the same action forever. No-progress detection watches recent actions and halts on the third identical one, saving the remaining steps and tokens.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is a max-step cap not sufficient loop safety by itself?
options: Step caps slow the agent down
It bounds iterations but not tokens, time, or cost — a few huge-context steps can still be slow and expensive
It prevents the model from finishing
checkpoints.explanation: A step cap only limits how many turns run. It can't see that each turn adds tokens (money) and seconds (latency), so a handful of large-context or slow-tool steps can blow cost and time budgets. You need token, time, and cost limits alongside it.

checkpoints.prompt: What distinguishes a 'clean' agent stop from a forced one?
options: A clean stop happens when the token budget runs out
A clean stop comes from an explicit done signal (finish/final_answer); caps, budgets, and no-progress are forced fallback stops
A forced stop always throws an exception
checkpoints.explanation: Clean success is the agent deliberately signaling completion (a finish tool or final_answer). Hitting a step cap, budget, or no-progress guard is a forced stop the caller handles differently — often routing to a human or fallback rather than treating it as a finished task.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the guard so a stuck agent halts once the same action repeats three times.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
recent.append(action)
if len(recent) >= 3 and recent[-1] == recent[-2] ==
checkpoints.explanation: Comparing recent[-1] == recent[-2] == recent[-3] checks the last three actions are identical — a no-progress signal — so the loop halts early instead of spinning to the step cap.

theory.question: Why does every autonomous agent loop need guardrails, and what are the core ones?
theory.directAnswer: Because the agent decides its own next action, nothing inherently stops it — an ungoverned loop can run forever, exhaust context, hang on a slow tool, or burn unbounded money, and a single model mistake or prompt injection can trigger any of these unattended. The core guardrails are a max-step cap, token and wall-clock time budgets, no-progress (repetition) detection, an explicit done signal for clean completion, and a hard cost cap as the last line of defense.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered set of termination and resource controls wrapped around the agent's decision loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Self-directed control flow means the loop's stopping behavior isn't guaranteed by the code structure, so you impose explicit bounds on iterations, resources, and cost.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Loop over a fixed range (step cap), check a token counter and a monotonic deadline each turn, track recent actions to detect no progress, treat only an explicit finish action as clean success, and estimate spend to abort at a cost ceiling — each limit producing a handled, routable outcome.

theory.whyImportant: These controls are what make an autonomous agent affordable, predictable, and safe enough to run unattended in production.
theory.realWorldExample: A research agent given an open query was capped at 12 steps, a 30s deadline, and a $0.50 ceiling; when a search tool started rate-limiting, the run hit the time budget and returned a partial result with a 'time budget' reason instead of hanging or overspending.

followUps.question: Which guardrail catches waste that budgets miss?
followUps.answer: No-progress detection — an agent can stay under every budget while repeating the same action, and only tracking recent actions/state catches that early.

followUps.question: How should a forced stop be surfaced?
followUps.answer: As a structured outcome with a reason (cap/budget/no-progress) that the caller routes to a human, a fallback, or a safe default — never an unhandled exception.

theory.question: How do you control the cost of an autonomous agent, and why isn't a step cap enough?
theory.directAnswer: Track spend directly — tokens map to money — and abort at a hard per-run cost cap, ideally with alerts before the ceiling and per-user limits too. A step cap alone is insufficient because cost scales with tokens per step, not step count: a few turns with a large accumulated context can cost more than many small turns, and a slow or looping run can quietly rack up spend. Combine the step cap with token budgets and an explicit cost ceiling.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cost-governance layer that estimates and bounds the money a single run (and a user) can spend.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Autonomous loops can be triggered adversarially or drift into expensive behavior, and token pricing means uncontrolled context growth becomes real, unbounded spend.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Accumulate tokens per turn, convert to an estimated dollar cost with the model's price, halt when it crosses the cap, and layer per-run and per-user ceilings with alerting so a runaway is caught early rather than on the invoice.

theory.whyImportant: It prevents a single bad or malicious run from producing a shocking bill and makes agent spend predictable and attributable.
theory.realWorldExample: A prompt-injection attempt pushed an agent into a long tool-calling loop; the per-run cost cap aborted it at $0.50 with an alert, so the incident cost cents instead of hundreds of dollars.

followUps.question: Why cap per user as well as per run?
followUps.answer: A single user could launch many runs; per-user caps and rate limits stop aggregate spend from escaping even when each run is individually bounded.

followUps.question: What reduces cost before the cap even matters?
followUps.answer: Tighter tools, concise tool output, prompt caching of fixed prefixes, and no-progress detection all shrink tokens per run, lowering spend well under the ceiling.

scenario.question: A newly launched agent occasionally runs for many minutes and produces surprise cost spikes on some requests. How would you make it safe and predictable?
scenario.directAnswer: Instrument steps, tokens, time, and estimated cost per run so you can see the outliers, then add the full guardrail stack: a max-step cap, a wall-clock deadline, a token budget, no-progress detection, and a hard per-run and per-user cost cap with alerts. Ensure the model has an explicit finish action so clean completions are distinguishable, and make every forced stop a structured outcome routed to a fallback or human instead of hanging or crashing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reliability-and-cost hardening of an ungoverned agent loop exhibiting long runtimes and spend spikes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The long runs come from missing time/step bounds and no no-progress detection; the cost spikes come from unbounded token growth with no cost cap — both are the absence of loop-safety controls.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Add per-turn checks for a monotonic deadline and token budget, loop over a bounded range, track recent actions to halt spinning runs, accumulate estimated spend against a ceiling with alerting, and return a reasoned stop outcome the caller can route.

scenario.whyImportant: It converts unbounded, unpredictable runs into bounded, observable, and affordable ones — the prerequisite for running an agent unattended at scale.
scenario.realWorldExample: After adding a 30s deadline, a 12-step cap, no-progress detection, and a $0.50 cap with alerting, the p99 runtime dropped from minutes to seconds and the surprise spend spikes disappeared, replaced by clean 'budget reached' outcomes.

followUps.question: What metrics prove it's working?
followUps.answer: Track steps-per-run, tokens-per-run, wall-clock p50/p99, cost-per-run, and the rate of each stop reason; a rising forced-stop rate flags a regression or attack.

followUps.question: How do these guardrails relate to no-progress and ReAct loops?
followUps.answer: They're the same safety layer: ReAct's rambling/repetition pitfalls are precisely what no-progress detection plus step/token/cost caps bound.

keyTakeaways: An autonomous agent chooses its own next step, so without guardrails it can loop forever, exhaust context, hang, or overspend.
Start with a max-step cap (loop over a fixed range, not while True) so even a non-terminating agent halts after N turns.
Add token and wall-clock budgets, because a few large-context or slow steps can blow cost and latency that a step count can't see.
Use no-progress detection to catch a spinning agent early and an explicit done signal to distinguish clean success from a forced stop.
Enforce a hard cost cap (per run and per user, with alerts) as the last line of defense against runaway or prompt-injection loops.
